summary: Alabama doesn't name Rattus rattus anywhere, and the whole question turns on one classification: is your captive-bred roof rat a 'domestic animal' or a 'wild rodent'? State health rules (ADPH r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) define a 'domestic animal' as one bred through human association to the point of genetic changes in temperament/color/conformation — so a pedigreed, captive-bred, color-mutation roof rat can qualify, and if it does, keeping/breeding/selling are unregulated at the state level. If it's instead treated as a 'wild rodent,' the wildlife rule (Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26) is harsh: it bans importing a wild rodent from out of state AND bans transporting one within the state at all (even an Alabama-born animal) except by a licensed game-breeder. There's no R. rattus-specific safe harbor, so the practical risk is an officer disagreeing that your animal is 'domestic.' Importing a domestic pet rat needs an electronic health certificate (eCVI); a 'semi-wild' classification adds a 10-day State-Veterinarian notice. Get a written ADCNR classification before importing or selling.

kit.problem:
Alabama law never mentions the roof rat (Rattus rattus) by name. There is no pet-rodent permit, no statewide ban, and no list that puts the species on or off limits. Instead, everything hinges on one classification question: is your captive-bred, tame pet roof rat a "domestic animal" or a "wild rodent"?

Alabama's public-health rule (Ala. Admin. Code r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) defines a "domestic animal" as one bred through human association to the point of genetic changes in temperament, color, or conformation that distinguish it from wild animals of the same species. A pedigreed, captive-bred, color-mutation roof rat that has never lived in the wild fits that test. If it is "domestic," keeping, breeding, and giving it away are unregulated by the state, and you can take it to the vet freely.

But Alabama's wildlife rule (Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26) is harsh toward any "wild rodent": it bans importing one from out of state, bans selling one, and bans ALL transport within the state — even an Alabama-born animal, even a trip to the vet — except by a licensed game breeder. Because no Alabama rule names R. rattus as an exempt domestic pet, every owner carries the burden of proving their tame animal is "domestic," and a single officer could decide to treat the whole species as a restricted "wild rodent." That uncertainty is the problem.
kit.ask: Ask the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources (Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries Division) for a written interpretation confirming that a pedigreed, captive-bred Rattus rattus exhibiting domestication traits (genetic docility and domestic color mutations) is a "domestic animal" under ADPH Rule 420-4-4-.01(6) — and therefore exempt from the possession, sale, and intrastate-transport bans of r. 220-2-.26 — rather than a restricted "wild rodent." That classification turns on domestication, not wild ancestry: the dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet Alabama treats both as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness, not their wild origins — exactly the genetic-change test the ADPH rule describes — and a pedigreed captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense. We ask the Division to weigh that question, not to reach a particular result. Even better, ask the agency to recognize pedigreed captive-bred Rattus as a category of domestic animal so individual owners no longer carry that burden case by case (New Jersey's genus-level exemption for Rattus is the model to cite). Separately, ask the Alabama Department of Agriculture and Industries (State Veterinarian) to confirm in writing that importing a captive-bred pet roof rat requires only a standard electronic Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (eCVI), not the 10-day "semi-wild animal" pre-report under r. 80-3-6-.23.
kit.branch_note:
This is branch (a): a BUREAUCRATIC CLASSIFICATION problem, and the lever is the AGENCY — not the legislature.

Here is why, concretely for Alabama. No statute and no administrative list names Rattus rattus. The restriction does not come from the species being placed on a prohibited list by the legislature; it comes entirely from how an agency might READ a generic, undefined phrase ("wild rodent" in r. 220-2-.26) against a separate definition of "domestic animal" (r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) that a captive-bred pet roof rat can already satisfy. The law as written actually contains the exemption we want — the "domestic animal" carve-out — so we are not asking anyone to change a law. We are asking the agency to apply the existing definition correctly and to say so in writing.

That makes the correct tool a written agency interpretation / declaratory ruling from ADCNR Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries (the body that administers r. 220-2-.26), optionally backed by ADPH (which owns the "domestic animal" definition) and ADAI's State Veterinarian (for the import question). A legislative campaign would be the wrong tool here: there is no bad statute to repeal and no species on a statutory list to remove. Conversely, the honest caveat in the other direction: if ADCNR responds that it categorically treats R. rattus as a "wild rodent" regardless of captive-breeding history, then it would be applying r. 220-2-.26 in a way the rule's text arguably permits, and at that point the durable fix shifts to a rulemaking petition (asking ADCNR to amend 220-2-.26 to add a captive-bred-Rattus exemption) rather than a one-off appeal — because you cannot argue an agency out of a reading the rule lets it hold; you have to change the rule. Start with the clarification request; escalate to a rulemaking petition only if the agency confirms a categorical "wild rodent" reading.

template.en:
Subject: Request for written classification — captive-bred domestic roof rat (Rattus rattus)

To the Wildlife and Freshwater Fisheries Division:

I am writing to request a written interpretation of how Alabama classifies a pedigreed, captive-bred pet roof rat (Rattus rattus) kept as a household companion. My concern is the difference between a "domestic animal" under ADPH Rule 420-4-4-.01(6) and a restricted "wild rodent" under Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26.

These animals are captive-bred over many generations, tame, kept indoors only, and never released. They show the genetic changes in temperament and color that the "domestic animal" definition describes — much like the fancy rat sold in pet stores. The issue is not whether a wild-caught rat is wild; it is that a domesticated, captive-bred animal should be recognized as domestic. The dog descends from the wolf and the house cat from a wild felid, yet both are recognized as domestic animals because of generations bred for tameness, not their wild ancestry — and a captive-bred roof rat is domesticated in that same sense.

Would you please confirm in writing that such an animal is a "domestic animal" — and therefore exempt from the possession, sale, and intrastate-transport provisions of r. 220-2-.26 — so an owner needs no game-breeder license simply to keep one or take it to a veterinarian? If feasible, I would also welcome the Division recognizing pedigreed, captive-bred Rattus as a domestic category, as some other states have done, so owners are not left to prove this animal by animal.

Thank you for your time and guidance.

[Your name]
[Your city, Alabama]
[Your email / phone]

(b) The old jurisdiction file listed a license email (dcnr.wfflicense@...) and named individuals (State Vet, an import staffer); I did NOT use any individual's name and substituted the verified role-based Wildlife Section inbox and official forms, which is the safer, OPSEC-clean, and more durable channel. (c) No live bill, pending list, or open comment window exists for this issue, so time_sensitive is intentionally empty — no manufactured urgency. (d) This is a research aid, not legal advice.

keep.why: No Alabama statute names Rattus rattus, and there is no state pet-rodent permit. Legality turns on classification: ADPH r. 420-4-4-.01(6) defines a 'domestic animal' as one bred through human association to a degree producing genetic changes (temperament/color/conformation) distinguishing it from wild animals of its species; 'wildlife' (r. 420-4-4-.01(12)) is everything else. A pedigreed, captive-bred, color-mutation roof rat can meet the 'domestic' test → keeping is unregulated, no permit. But if an officer deems it a 'wild rodent,' ADCNR r. 220-2-.26 bars possession of one imported from out of state (in-state-trapped wild rodents fall to unprotected-nongame rules but then can't be transported — see transport). No species-specific exemption names R. rattus, so the owner carries the evidentiary burden of domestication.
keep.governing_law: Ala. Admin. Code r. 420-4-4-.01(6),(12) (ADPH domestic-vs-wild definitions); Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26 (ADCNR 'wild rodent' import/possession); Code of Ala. 1975 Title 9 ch. 11.

breed.why: Alabama has NO statewide commercial pet-breeder or small-rodent breeder license; if the animal is 'domestic,' non-commercial and hobby breeding are unregulated by the state. Commercial breeding is governed at the LOCAL/municipal level (e.g., the City of Gadsden's Commercial Breeder Permit + business license) — check your city/county. If the rat is instead classed as a 'wild rodent,' breeding it for transport/sale requires an ADCNR Game Breeder license (Code of Ala. §9-11-30; ~$250/yr non-cervid; facility inspections). Federally, USDA AWA exempts face-to-face/retail and small hobby sellers; the >4-breeding-female wholesale/sight-unseen threshold is the federal commercial demarcation (no Alabama state threshold).
breed.governing_law: No statewide pet-breeder statute; local municipal ordinances; Code of Ala. §9-11-30 (Game Breeder — only if 'wild'); USDA AWA (federal).

sell_give.why: Alabama has no state-level pet-dealer/pet-shop licensing act for domestic small animals; selling a 'domestic' pet rat needs only a standard retail revenue/business license for a storefront (Ala. Dept of Revenue 'Pet Shop' code), and private/free transfer is unregulated. BUT 220-2-.26 expressly prohibits the sale of a 'wild rodent' — so if the animal is classed wild, sale/transfer is banned. Everything again hinges on the domestic-vs-wild classification.
sell_give.governing_law: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26 (no sale of 'wild rodent'); Ala. Code Title 40/Dept of Revenue retail license; no state pet-dealer act.

transport.why: INTRASTATE: ADCNR r. 220-2-.26(1) bans transporting a 'wild rodent' anywhere within Alabama — explicitly 'whether such member originated within or without the state' — EXCEPT by a properly licensed game-breeder. So if the animal is classed 'wild,' even a vet trip is unlawful; only the 'domestic animal' classification (or a game-breeder license) makes intrastate transport legal/unregulated. IMPORT (legal_with_permit): a domestic pet rat entering Alabama needs an electronic Certificate of Veterinary Inspection (eCVI via Global Vet Link or AgView; paper APHIS Form 7001 prohibited since 2019; valid 30 days). A 'semi-wild' classification additionally triggers a 10-day advance notice to the State Veterinarian (r. 80-3-6-.23); a 'wild rodent' classification = import banned. EXPORT: unregulated by Alabama (meet the destination state's rules; USFWS Form 3-177 for international, since the federal government treats R. rattus as wildlife). Never release. Net: 'restricted' because the binding intrastate ban + the import paperwork both turn on a classification the state hasn't settled for R. rattus.
transport.governing_law: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.26(1) (intrastate 'wild rodent' transport ban); ADAI eCVI import policy; Ala. Admin. Code r. 80-3-6-.23 (10-day semi-wild pre-report); USFWS Form 3-177 (intl export).

restrictions.summary: Everything turns on whether your roof rat is a 'domestic animal' (ADPH genetic-change test, r. 420-4-4-.01(6)) or a 'wild rodent' (ADCNR r. 220-2-.26). If 'domestic': keeping/breeding/selling are state-unregulated and intrastate transport is legal; import needs an eCVI. If 'wild': import, sale, and ALL intrastate transport are barred except via a game-breeder license. Get a written ADCNR classification before importing or selling, and keep pedigree/photos documenting captive breeding + color mutations.
steps: Ask ADCNR (WFF) in writing whether a pedigreed, captive-bred R. rattus is a 'domestic animal' or a restricted 'wild rodent' under 220-2-.26
For import: obtain an electronic CVI (Global Vet Link or AgView) from a USDA-accredited vet (valid 30 days); ask ADAI whether the 10-day State-Vet pre-report (80-3-6-.23) applies
For commercial breeding/sale: check your city/county for a local commercial-breeder permit + business license
Keep documentation (pedigree, photos of domestic color mutations) to support the 'domestic animal' classification
restrictions.where_to_file: Alabama DCNR (Wildlife & Freshwater Fisheries — classification); Alabama Dept of Agriculture & Industries (State Veterinarian — eCVI/import); local animal control (commercial breeding)

restrictions.summary: Never release a roof rat — releasing any captive-raised/non-indigenous mammal into the wild in Alabama is illegal without express written ADCNR Commissioner permission, and it's ecologically harmful. Rehome responsibly.

inquiry_focus: We want a written interpretation of the domestic-vs-wild classification for a captive-bred, domesticated Rattus rattus kept as a pet: (a) Does ADCNR Law Enforcement recognize a pedigreed, captive-bred R. rattus that exhibits genetic docility and phenotypic variation (e.g., domestic color mutations) as a 'domestic animal' under ADPH Rule 420-4-4-.01(6), or does it categorically treat the species as a restricted 'wild rodent' under r. 220-2-.26 regardless of captive-breeding history? (b) If classified 'domestic,' is it fully exempt from the possession AND intrastate-transport bans of 220-2-.26 (so an owner needs no game-breeder license to take it to a vet)? (c) For importing a captive-bred pet roof rat into Alabama, is it treated as a standard domestic pet needing only an eCVI, or as a 'semi-wild animal' triggering the 10-day prior notice to the State Veterinarian under r. 80-3-6-.23?
